entries.content:
Pratik Bhangale

Product Manager, Google Cloud

Agents represent a fundamental shift in cloud operations. They can act on behalf of users or autonomously, make non-deterministic decisions, and request data across projects at unprecedented speed and scale. Because agents are a distinct category of non-human identity (NHI), they require unique secure-by-default guardrails.

Traditional, manually-operated network perimeters are vulnerable to today’s machine-speed attacks. Overly permissive perimeters, built to avoid blocked connections, increase the risk of unauthorized data theft, but overly strict perimeters stall development under a flood of access denials.

Today, we're excited to announce key enhancements to VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) that make perimeters easier to create, maintain, and scale. You can now add folders to perimeter membership, so that projects contained in them inherit policy. You can also manage granular exceptions and resolve denials with guided, scoped remediation. 

The result is data protected by default, so you can scale autonomous agents across your enterprise without letting data leave your perimeter. This update is generally available, and at no additional cost.

Perimeters aligned to your architecture

VPC-SC provides a context-aware network security perimeter around your Google Cloud deployment, designed to secure your organization against data theft, even in the event of compromised credentials, identity and access management (IAM) misconfigurations, and insider threats. By extending network-layer protection across service-to-service interactions in Google Cloud's infrastructure, VPC-SC goes beyond traditional firewalls and creates an additional layer of defense that prevents access outside your corporate network — and is now easier for your organization to manage.

Cloud administrators configuring VPC-SC can now include folders in perimeter membership, automatically extending the folder’s access policy to every project and nested subfolder it contains. New workloads can inherit protection by default, with no further modification.

Figure 1: Simplified perimeter authoring in VPC-SC.

Perimeter membership updates when a project is moved, simplifying lifecycle maintenance. Security coverage follows the resource hierarchy that your organization already governs, and compliance verification requires only confirming that the resource is located in the correct part of the hierarchy.

Dry-run mode also supports folder membership, helping administrators evaluate the effect of a hierarchy-wide perimeter against live traffic before enforcement.

Folder and organization support in ingress and egress rules

Well-defined ingress and egress rules establish granular, context-aware perimeters without sacrificing operational flexibility across complex multi-project environments. Security administrators can now specify Google Cloud folders and organizations directly within those rules. A single hierarchy reference stands in for the set of projects beneath it, which keeps rules concise, keeps attribute counts well within quota limits, and extends access automatically to projects created later in the hierarchy.

Figure 2 : Simplified authoring of ingress/egress rules.

Using Private Service Connect endpoints in ingress and egress rules

Enterprises increasingly use private paths to reach desired endpoints in their deployment instead of exposing the traffic to the internet. Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs are now supported as an attribute in ingress and egress rules. Administrators can author a rule that authorizes access specifically over a designated private endpoint, producing a policy that corresponds directly to the connectivity architecture it is intended to govern.

Figure 3: Supporting Private Service Connect endpoints with ingress and egress rules.

For organizations that have standardized on Private Service Connect, including endpoints propagated across the estate through Network Connectivity Center, this provides both a more precise and a more concise means of expressing source for the request.

Service patterns in VPC accessible services

Service patterns in VPC accessible services provide granular control over Google APIs accessed with private Virtual IP addresses (VIP), permitting interoperability beyond just VPC-SC integrated services. If the workload requires controlled access to validated API endpoints over a private path, administrators can now allow only the specific API URL patterns required. 

Additionally, the capability supports appending org-restriction-headers with egress requests to facilitate access to only authorized domains and resources. Because you don’t need to manage egress-proxy, you can accommodate legitimate operational requirements while maintaining a tightly-bounded private path, instead of choosing between a broad allowance and no access at all.

Figure 4: Granular control over Google APIs with service patterns in VPC accessible services.

Guided violation remediation

VPC-SC perimeter policies evolve continuously alongside the workloads they protect, and administrators periodically need to authorize a legitimate access request not yet covered. New Guided Violation Remediation in VPC-SC Violation Analyzer cuts resolution time for blocked requests from days to minutes by generating a policy fix with remediation recommendations, which you can validate in Dry-Run mode first. 

Rather than just diagnosing why the violation occurred for a given denial, Violation Analyzer evaluates the blocked request against the applicable perimeter configuration, and proposes a specific configuration change, narrowly scoped by least-privilege design principles, to authorize the traffic: an ingress rule, an egress rule, an access level, or an update to VPC accessible services. This relieves pressure on administrators to broadly open up a perimeter just to resolve a violation and get an application working quickly.

Read more about how BlackLine uses Violation Analyzer to streamline investigations.

Figure 5 : VPC-SC Violation Remediation for faster turn-around.

Get started today

VPC-SC makes it simple and automated to deploy and refine granular network perimeter protection, even for autonomous agents. To get started:

  • Establish your folder baseline: Identify the folders in your resource hierarchy that correspond to the boundaries you intend to enforce, and define perimeters around them so that new workloads inherit policy on creation.

  • Run risk-free in Dry-Run mode: Observe production traffic safely without blocking active developers.

  • Unblock traffic with Violation Analyzer and Violation Dashboard: Use automated least-privilege remediation recommendations to resolve any denials that surface.

  • Enforce with confidence: Secure your full data estate by transitioning to enforcement once your dry-run logs show your intended access with clean, authorized traffic.

To learn more about how VPC-SC can help simplify your data security posture and confidently secure your autonomous agent fleets, check out the VPC-SC documentation.

entries.title: How Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs
entries.summary: Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days. What makes a live video
entries.content:
Will Yin

CEO, Visko

Ivan Nardini

Developer Relations Engineer, Google Cloud

Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days.

What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock. Unlike offline video generators where a user submits a prompt and waits in a queue, a live world model streams continuously. Every new chunk of video and synchronized audio must finish rendering before the viewer finishes watching the previous one, or the world freezes.

Today, we're excited to share how Visko, an AI startup pioneering interactive world models, teamed up with Google Cloud to solve this exact challenge. Working side by side, Visko and Google Cloud engineers deployed Visko's end-to-end live inference pipeline — combining video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio—onto a single Cloud TPU slice. Together, the teams brought end-to-end generation down, rendering at 1.07x playback speed.

Here is an inside look at how we engineered the pipeline to hit that milestone in a single month, the architectural optimizations that moved the needle, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI on Google Cloud.

Redefining interactive media with Live World Models

While most generative video platforms focus on rendering fixed, pre-baked clips, Visko is building what it calls Live Models: video world models that generate continuously and respond on the fly.

Visko's flagship model, Orbis, streams live video starting from a single text or image prompt. As the stream plays, viewers can enter new steering prompts in real time, dynamically evolving the scene without restarting or breaking continuity. For instance, in one test session, the livestream opens on a cat napping beside a crackling fireplace; when the viewer steers the scene to introduce a bowl of food, the bowl materializes seamlessly, and the cat stretches, stands up, and meows.

Since launching its public demo on September 1, 2026, Orbis has unlocked new possibilities across interactive entertainment, live commerce, AI companions, immersive education, and robotics simulation. To scale these interactive sessions reliably, Visko partnered with Google Cloud TPU engineers in August 2026 to port the Orbis live pipeline to Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). Within 30 days, the full multimodal pipeline was running in real time on TPUs.

Visko’s ambition is to power a new generation of interactive worlds that people can step into and shape in real time. Streaming continuous video and audio under a strict clock is a fundamentally different system challenge than offline clip generation. Working side by side with Google Cloud's TPU engineers, we brought the full Orbis pipeline to TPUs in just 30 days — giving us the low-latency compute and memory bandwidth required to bring Live Models to creators and developers at scale.

"Visko is bringing an exciting new class of real-time, steerable workloads to the Cloud TPU ecosystem. By co-engineering their live multimodal pipeline on a singleTPU slice using JAX, torchax, and custom Pallas kernels, we proved how quickly a lean startup team can go from PyTorch prototype to render at 1.07x playback speed on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer."

– Dave Elliott, Head of Developer Advocacy for AI, Google Cloud 

Live video is a hard-deadline problem

When you serve an offline clip generator, latency is forgiving — the user waits once while the backend processes frames. A live world model has no waiting room.

Every single chunk must be denoised, decoded from latents, upscaled to 1664x936 (at 18 fps), and paired with generated audio faster than realtime playback speed, for as long as the session runs.

Two structural constraints make live world models far more demanding than standard batch inference:

  • Batch size of one: Each live stream represents an individual viewer's interactive session. You cannot mask latency by grouping dozens of concurrent requests into a massive batch — the standard playbook for keeping AI accelerators saturated.

  • Strict sequential dependency: Every chunk depends directly on the one before it. Because the video model maintains a rolling memory of recent video latents so that chunk N+1 smoothly continues the action from chunk N, you cannot pre-render chunks out of order or parallelize across future timestamps.

For startup infrastructure engineers coming from LLM serving, it helps to think of live world modeling not as a tokens-per-second throughput benchmark, but as an unforgiving per-step latency SLO.

Architecting the multimodal pipeline on a single TPU slice

To keep infrastructure lean and cost-effective as Visko scales, the team designed the live pipeline to chain three distinct generative models on a single Cloud TPU slice running in BF16 precision.

When a viewer submits an initial prompt or a live steering update, all three generative models — the core video diffusion model, the super-resolution upscaler, and the audio generator — share the same chips, taking turns on the hardware for each chunk.

Figure 1: Visko's end-to-end Orbis live pipeline chains video diffusion, latent decoding, super-resolution upscaling, and pure-JAX audio generation sequentially on a single Cloud TPU slice, completing each chunk faster than the playback speed.

To combine rapid startup iteration with bare-metal accelerator speed, the software stack is built on three open-source pillars:

  • JAX: Google's high-performance Python array library for accelerators, compiled into optimized machine code by the XLA compiler.

  • torchax: An interoperability layer that runs PyTorch models directly on Cloud TPUs via JAX, enabling startup teams to bring existing PyTorch components over without an upfront, ground-up rewrite.

  • Pallas: The custom kernel programming language for TPUs in JAX.

Real-time performance breakdown: Hitting the clock

By profiling and optimizing each stage on a single slice in BF16, the engineering team achieved a total per-chunk latency of under the target while — maintaining roughly 7% headroom to absorb variance during live streaming:

Figure 2: Chart of per-chunk latency budget on one TPU slice.

Because video denoising accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total compute budget, that stage became the primary focus of our kernel and parallelism optimizations.

Inside the stack: Three optimizations that unlocked real-time streaming

1. Ulysses context parallelism across all TPU chips

A video chunk expands into a massive sequence of spatiotemporal tokens inside the video transformer. To distribute that workload across the TPU chips at batch size 1, the team implemented Ulysses context parallelism.

Instead of splitting model weights, Ulysses splits the token sequence across chips. Immediately before the attention layer, a high-speed all-to-all interconnect exchange regroups the tensors so that each chip holds the entire video sequence, but only for one-quarter of the attention heads. After each chip computes attention over the full sequence for its assigned heads, a second all-to-all exchange restores the sequence-split layout for the feed-forward layers.

Figure 3: Ulysses context parallelism across TPU chips at batch size 1. High-speed all-to-all Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) exchanges transition tensors between a sequence-split layout for feed-forward layers and a head-split layout for Pallas splash attention.

2. Custom Pallas splash attention from MaxDiffusion

To accelerate the attention computation itself, the team integrated a custom Pallas splash attention kernel from MaxDiffusion, Google Cloud's open-source reference library for diffusion models on Cloud TPU.

Splash attention brings FlashAttention-style tiling to TPU architecture: rather than materializing the full quadratic attention matrix in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), it computes attention in compact tiles that remain inside ultra-fast on-chip VMEM. Startup teams can drop the exact kernel used in this port straight into their own pipelines via custom_splash_attention.py.

3. A 5.8x audio speedup by moving from torchax to pure JAX

We first brought all three Orbis models onto Cloud TPU with torchax, which runs PyTorch code on TPU through JAX and XLA without a rewrite. For the video and upscaling models, torchax paired with Pallas attention kernels met our latency target directly, and both stay in torchax in the final pipeline.

Only the audio model needed a rewrite. Moving the audio stage from torchax to native JAX made it 5.8x faster and brought the full pipeline under the playback deadline.

Field notes for AI builders: Cloud TPU lessons

Takeaways from tuning live multimodal inference on Cloud TPU:

  • Ulysses context parallelism for single stream video: At batch size 1, splitting the token sequence across chips with all-to-all interconnect exchanges was faster than both tensor parallelism and ring attention.
  • Native BF16 for continuous streams: FP8 quantization cuts memory bandwidth pressure, but small quantization errors build up across chunks in a continuous stream. Native BF16 kept visual quality intact within the latency budget.
  • Selective JAX ports: torchax kept the video and upscaling models in PyTorch, so the team only rewrote the audio bottleneck in native JAX.
  • XLA compilation caching: The first boot spends a few minutes compiling XLA graphs. Caching compiled artifacts brings worker restarts under a minute.

Building real-time generative models on Cloud TPU? Start here

If your startup is pushing the boundaries of live video, world models, or ultra-low-latency multimodal inference, you can build with the same toolkit that powered Visko's port:

  • Accelerate diffusion attention out of the box: Grab the open-source splash attention kernel used in this collaboration from MaxDiffusion, and explore the Pallas documentation to write custom TPU kernels.

  • Migrate PyTorch fast, then optimize selectively: Bring your existing PyTorch models onto TPU quickly with torchax, pinpoint bottlenecks with the Cloud TPU Profiler, and port latency-critical stages to native JAX.

  • Spin up TPUs on demand: Use TPU Flex-start VMs to provision TPU capacity for short development and benchmarking runs without a long-term reservation.

  • Scale with Google for Startups: Early-stage AI startups looking for cloud credits, technical mentorship, and access to Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer stack can apply to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.

Special thanks to the Visko.ai team for the close technical partnership, and to the Google Cloud TPU engineers who lead the project including: Yixin Shi, James Huang, and Elisa Tsai.

entries.title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust
entries.summary: Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram Introduction On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot
entries.content:
Google Threat Intelligence Group
Mandiant

Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram

Introduction

On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files.

During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders.

Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public.

Exploitation

Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the 

/home
directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog.

Post-Exploitation

Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection.

Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events

Staging Webshell

After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to 

/app_84304470%2Ephp
. Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path 
/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/
. ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion. 

SAWFLY Webshell

SAWFLY (

mangoapi.php
) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter 
_c94mfe
. 

If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found (

http_response_code(404)
) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the 
_c94mfe
parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via 
@eval()
. Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client. 

Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions

The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable (

/bin/sh
) to the file 
/usr/bin/dbus-authd
.

The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system.

After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset.

Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction

Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the 

/ns/sbin/bt-secrets
binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials.

The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault:

/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault
/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault
/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault

Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs

First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile.

Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials.

The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored in 

/home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log
and any archived files.
/usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;'

Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs

Persistence

For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account.

First, the threat actor created the 

/home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d
directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named 
zz-root-persist
.

The contents of the 

zz-root-persist
script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the 
/ns/config/sudoers.template
file. If the entry is missing, the script appends
 
'%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL'
to the template. This entry added  to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system.

Finally, the script executes

 
'/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc
, which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse 
/ns/config/sudoers.template
and rebuild the active 
/etc/sudoers
file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to 
/etc/sudoers
.
#!/bin/bash
grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template'
'/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc

Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist

Anti-Forensics

Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs.

Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories:

'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*'

Figure 5: Recovered Command

Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse

After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal.

{
  "event": "login",
  "status": "success",
  "target": "web/login",
  "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password",
  "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]"
}

Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry

After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from 

No Access
to 
Administrator
. Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list.

{
  "event": "user_changed",
  "old_username": "[REDACTED]",
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1,
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3,
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access",
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator",
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1,
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3,
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access",
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator"
}

Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry

Internal Reconnaissance

Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints.

Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment.

BARECLAW Tunneler

Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default.

BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu:

Usage: %s [options]
  --listen PORT            plain ws port (default 8080)
  --listen-tls PORT        wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert)
  --ssl-cert FILE          PEM certificate (enables wss)
  --token STRING           shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed)
  --obfs                   enable XOR stream obfuscation
  --timeout SEC            idle timeout (default 300)
  --connect-timeout SEC    target connect timeout (default 10)
  --max-tunnels N          concurrent tunnel limit (default 100)
  --allow-net CIDR         allowed target subnet (repeatable)
  --upstream [socks5://]host:port   route via upstream SOCKS5
  --threads N              civetweb worker threads (default 64)
  --ws-path PATH           websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy)
  -q, --quiet              zero output (all logging suppressed)
  -h                       this help

Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu

The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments:

/tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge

Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments

This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint 

/uidchanarge
on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance.

Modifications to Haproxy.conf

In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the 

/ns/config/haproxy.conf
file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path. 

The 

haproxy.conf
file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named 
wswsws
to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path 
/uidchanarge
. When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as 
webskd3
.
    acl wswsws path /uidchanarge
    use_backend webskd3 if wswsws

Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf

Next, the 

webskd3
backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection.
backend webskd3
    mode http
    server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800
    option http-keep-alive
    timeout server 28s
    timeout tunnel 5h

Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf

Attribution

GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE.

GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations. 

Outlook and Implications

In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764.

GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887. 

Remediation and Hardening

Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog. CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations.

Immediate Mitigation

Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs.

Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended)

  • Remote Support SaaS: BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply.

  • Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the 

    /appliance
    interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates.

  • Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1: Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure.

  • If the patch is not visible in 

    /appliance
    , open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05.

Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances

  • Preserve before acting: Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident.

  • Isolate at the perimeter: Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in 

    /appliance
    , so the configuration remains intact for review.

  • Restrict egress: Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection.

  • Terminate access paths: End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from 

    /login
    . Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives.

  • Rebuild rather than clean: Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance.

Note: Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding.

Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls

The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch.

Part A: Network Restrictions

  • Restrict access to the 

    /login
    and 
    /appliance
    administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet.

  • Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter.

Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review

  • Revoke sessions and enrollments: End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens.

  • Rotate credentials in dependency order: 

    /appliance
    administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window.

  • Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline: user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner.

  • Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting.

Note: Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance.

Part C: Control Plane Restrictions

  • Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all 

    /login
    users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use.

  • Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines.

  • Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user.

  • Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule.

  • Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance.

  • Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers.

Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering

Logging and Visibility

  • Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address.

  • Export 

    /login
    session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule.

Detection Engineering

  • Account and policy changes: 

    user_changed
    events that raise a Jump Item or team role; 
    user_added
    , 
    api_account
    , and 
    security_provider
    events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations.

  • Authentication: 

    /login
    success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours.

  • Session activity: file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window.

  • Request paths: at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges.

  • Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users.

File Indicators

Detections

YARA Rules

rule G_Hunting_Webshell_SAWFLY_1 {
  meta:
author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group"    
  strings:
    $b32 = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567" ascii wide
    $rc4 = "range(0,255)" ascii wide
    $pack = "pack('H*'," ascii wide
    $eval = "@eval(" ascii wide
    $code404 = "http_response_code(404)" ascii wide
  condition:
    filesize < 20KB and
    all of them
}
rule G_Hunting_Backdoor_BARECLAW_1 {
  meta:
    author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group"

  strings:
    $s1 = "[%s ws_socks5d] " ascii wide
    $s2 = "--obfs requires --token" ascii wide
    $s3 = "mux: %s (frame[%lu]: %s)" ascii wide
    $s4 = "cannot create stream pump/writer thread (stream %d)" ascii wide
    $s5 = "reject: bad or missing token from %s" ascii wide
    $s6 = "listening on %s path=%s (token=%s obfs=%s max_tunnels=%d threads=%d)" ascii wide
    $s7 = "--ws-path must start with '/'" ascii wide
    $b_xorshift = { 48 c1 e0 17 48 31 c1 48 89 f0 48 c1 e8 1a 48 31 f0 48 31 c8 48 c1 e9 11 48 31 c8 }
  condition:
    uint32(0) == 0x464c457f and (5 of ($s*)) or ($b_xorshift and (3 of ($s*)))
}

Google Security Operations (SecOps)

Google SecOps customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Mandiant Hunting, Mandiant Frontline Threats, and Mandiant Intel Emerging Threats rule packs. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names:

  • Echo Pipes Base64 To Shell

  • Base64 Encoded Shell Command Execution

  • Low Severity Endpoint Detection Cluster on Host

  • Suspicious Curl Download to tmp

  • Suspicious Curl Network Connection to Staging Directory

Acknowledgements

We appreciate BeyondTrust for their collaboration against this threat.

Welcome to the first Cloud CISO Perspectives for October 2026. Today, Stephanie Kiel explains the latest on our approach to post-quantum cryptography, and shares a new tool to help CISOs and executives prepare their organizations for PQC.

As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog. If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here.

New Gemini Notebook can help CISOs and policymakers prepare for PQC

By Stephanie Kiel, Head of Cloud Security Policy, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Google Cloud

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is one of the most urgent security shifts of the decade — and one of the easiest to tune out. For security leaders and policymakers, the research is dense, scattered across papers and engineering blogs, and can be challenging to turn into action.

To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. Ask it questions, listen to an audio overview, or test yourself with flashcards, and quickly get up to speed on the quantum threat.

Why PQC matters now

Quantum computing is rapidly moving from theory to reality. Our Willow chip and Quantum Echoes algorithm mark substantial progress, and Google research estimates that breaking ECDLP-256 and RSA-2048 encryption — the public-key cryptography schemes protecting much of our online data — would require around 500,000 and 1 million imperfect quantum computer components (noisy qubits), respectively.

To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place.

This research has consequences now. It indicates that today’s online security is more vulnerable to future quantum computers than previously thought.

In Store Now, Decrypt Later attacks, adversaries may steal encrypted data now and wait to decrypt it once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists. Data that we’ve long considered sensitive — health records, financial data, intellectual property, and government secrets — is already at risk. 

With continued advances in architecture, quantum algorithms, and quantum error correction shrinking future quantum hardware requirements, waiting to upgrade our digital locks is not a viable option. To help organizations stay ahead of the curve, Google has published a migration timeline noting our plans to transition to PQC by 2029, and we urge others to consider the same.

As the technology advances, policymakers should consider urging critical infrastructure owners and operators to recognize condensed timelines, and build PQC readiness into existing risk mitigation plans. We also recommend governments engage with global counterparts to promote a harmonized approach to standards development, and include technical and security experts in the building of policy and regulatory requirements focused on quantum safety.

Google's PQC expertise, in one notebook

The Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography notebook turns years of Google expertise into an interactive primer that anyone can use. It's built on curated Google sources covering the quantum era, quantum computing breakthroughs like Willow, Quantum Echoes, and surface code error suppression, industry PQC standards, Google's own deployments, and the latest research.

In the Gemini Notebook, you can:

  • Get answers grounded in Google's sources.

  • Listen to a podcast-style audio overview.

  • Test your PQC knowledge with flashcards.

  • Explore an interactive visual diagram of the quantum threat.

  • Read a concise briefing document.

Try these prompts

To get started, here are a few questions to ask the notebook:

  • For CISOs: "What should a CISO prioritize in the first 90 days of a PQC migration?"

  • For anyone new to PQC: "Explain store-now-decrypt-later in plain terms."

  • For developers: "How does hybrid ML-KEM key exchange work in Chrome?"

As with all generative AI, the notebook can make mistakes, so check its responses against the linked sources.

What's at stake

Previous cryptographic migrations, such as moving from SHA-1 or upgrading TLS, have taken a decade or more. Waiting for the availability of a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer before beginning the migration journey represents a significant security risk given the importance of public-key cryptography for securing digital essentials like web traffic, software updates, digital identities, and signatures.

For CISOs, we recommend that you start by:

  • Understanding where vulnerable cryptography lives in your organization.

  • Identifying and prioritizing data and systems most at risk from quantum threats, and developing a plan for addressing these risks.

  • Anticipate system-wide effects that PQC migration could have.

  • Building crypto-agility into your security plans, using learnings from past experiences like Heartbleed.

Additional detail on these recommendations is available in our previous blog post.  

For the broader security community, the transition only succeeds if this knowledge is accessible to everyone — not just organizations with dedicated cryptography teams.

How Google is putting PQC into practice

We’ve been deploying PQC for years. Highlights include:

  • Hybrid Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange protecting Chrome traffic

  • PQC in Android

  • Quantum-safe digital signatures in Cloud KMS

  • PQC for Google's internal communications

  • Wiz PQC readiness scanner across code, cloud, and runtime

We also co-founded the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance at the Linux Foundation with industry leaders including Amazon Web Services, Cisco, IBM, and NVIDIA to support open-source tools like Open Quantum Safe.

Build a PQC notebook for your own team

Here’s how you can create a resource similar to our PQC Gemini Notebook, specific to your organization’s needs:

  • Curate trusted sources. Start with a focused set of authoritative research, standards, and guidance.

  • Write neutral prompts. Keep instructions factual so outputs stay grounded in your sources.

  • Add AI disclaimers and a welcome note. Tell readers what the notebook covers and remind them that AI can make mistakes.

  • Review all output with human oversight. Have experts check every artifact before you share it.

Start preparing today

The quantum transition has already started, but preparing your organization doesn't have to begin with a 100-page whitepaper. Start by understanding the threat, then assess your cryptographic inventory and build a migration roadmap.

You can get started with the Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography Gemini Notebook and share it with your team today. To learn more about Google Cloud’s approach to PQC, check out our dedicated Google Cloud PQC Resource Hub.

In case you missed it

Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month:

  • Securing enterprise agility in the machine-speed era: Learn what executives need to know about today’s threat landscape, how security teams should respond, and why Google AI Threat Defense can help. Read more.
  • Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud: We’re making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, available for everyone on Google Cloud. Here’s how it can help boost the defender’s advantage. Read more.
  • Android's next-gen enclave for on-device AI: Learn about Android’s enclave architecture for personalized on-device AI experiences. Read more.
  • The Wiz Red Agent caught a Fortune 500 firm’s data exposure that other tools missed: Using an attacker’s mindset, the Red Agent found a public page exposing sensitive data in minutes. Read more.
  • Chrome's response to recent ccTLD registry hijacks: Following recent .gh, .sl, and .as ccTLD domain hijacks, Chrome immediately blocked unauthorized HTTPS certificates via CRLSets to protect users automatically. Read more.
  • Wiz Blue Agent POV: Investigating data theft across AWS and GitHub: See how the Blue Agent investigated a multi-platform attack in minutes, following evidence across AWS and GitHub to uncover compromised credentials, stolen source code, and custom data exfiltration tooling. Read more.
  • Introducing Wiz AI SAST: Application security that understands you: Find, validate, and fix complex business logic flaws with an AI code scanner backed by Wiz Research, operationalized in your existing security program. Read more.
  • Introducing WizOS Helm Charts to secure the Kubernetes supply chain: WizOS Helm Charts can help eliminate hidden CI/CD risks and unmaintained dependencies with hardened, signed, and CVE-scanned charts for Kubernetes. Read more.
  • What’s new in Wiz Service Catalog: Smarter discovery, governance, and service-level context can help build your service catalog faster, keep service context current, and give teams a clearer path from cloud risk to accountability. Read more.

Threat Intelligence news

Read more.
  • Defending against active exploitation of Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances: Mandiant Consulting and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified active, in-the-wild exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances. Here’s our containment and remediation guidance. Read more.
  • ShinyHunters renewed mass exploitation campaign targeting Oracle PeopleSoft: Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) have identified renewed mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by UNC6240 (ShinyHunters), along with expanded global targeting across multiple sectors. Read more.
  • Proactively defend by hardening code pipelines and CI/CD infrastructure: Check out our actionable blueprint for software and platform architects designed to safeguard the software supply chain against threat vectors that are actively being exploited, third-party risks, and architectural vulnerabilities throughout the entire software development lifecycle. , 
AI.SCORE
, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget proactively. 

We recently announced the general availability (GA) of token-based cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions: daily quotas that let administrators set self-serve guardrails on AI token consumption, so teams can innovate while staying within your budget. In this blog, we provide an overview of cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions, walk through a few practical examples, and share resources to help you get started. Let’s jump in.  

Quotas for managing costs

Four daily quotas, managed through the Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota system, provide controls at the project level and the per-user level. Per-user limits apply to each user within a project, not across your organization.

Key details:

  • The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching.

  • Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill.

Which functions are covered?

The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation:

  • AI.GENERATE

  • AI.GENERATE_TABLE

  • AI.GENERATE_TEXT
    (and its alias 
    ML.GENERATE_TEXT
    )

  • AI.CLASSIFY

  • AI.IF

  • AI.SCORE

  • AI.AGG

What's not covered: Embedding functions such as 

AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING
(also available as 
ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING
) and 
AI.EMBED
 are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models.

Managing your quotas

Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required.

  • Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

  • Filter by service and select BigQuery API.

  • Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top.

Locating the gen AI token quotas in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day.

5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota.

From there:

  • To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed.

  • To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review.

Editing a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner, Editor, Quota Administrator (

roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin
), or Service Usage Admin (
roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin
).

Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API, the 

gcloud
CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects.

Monitoring usage

Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage.

Daily project-level token usage for a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

Longer-term usage graph with selectable 7-day, 14-day, 30-day, and custom ranges.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas.

Token quotas vs. billing spend caps

Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud.

  • Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific. BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user.

  • Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred.

Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net.

How enforcement works

Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a 

QuotaExceeded
error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls:

  • Functions that support 

    max_error_ratio
    (such as 
    AI.IF
    ) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail.

  • General-purpose functions (such as 

    AI.GENERATE
    ) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their 
    status
    field contains the quota-exceeded error.

For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation.

Sizing your input data: 
AI.COUNT_TOKENS

To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The 

AI.COUNT_TOKENS
function helps with this.

AI.COUNT_TOKENS
returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data:

The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to:

  • Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it.

  • Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage.

  • Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model.

From tokens to budget: a worked example

Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount):

  • Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens

  • Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens

If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, you can solve for a daily budget:

Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates.

Best practices for managing AI cost

  • Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget.

  • Measure before you scale. Use 

    AI.COUNT_TOKENS
    to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits.

  • Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts 

    max_output_tokens
    , set it to bound generation length.

  • Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change.

Get started

Token-based cost management is available now. To begin:

  • Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API.

  • Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget.

  • Use 

    AI.COUNT_TOKENS
    to size your input data.

For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs.

With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

entries.content:
Praveen Kumar

Customer Engineer, Data & AI

The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting.

Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards.

BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue.

In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language.

Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration.

The borderless lakehouse architecture

This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms.

When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access:

  • Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define.

  • Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform.

All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service  for Apache Spark. Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution.

Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform.

You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below.

Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned service account:

Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal:

You must grant the 

EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA

Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details -

  • Issuer URL* -  https://accounts.google.com

  • Subject* - numeric subject ID returned by the catalog describe command eg 1124251400450xxxxxxxx

  • Audiences - https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com

Run one query across three clouds

Federated Iceberg tables are addressed in BigQuery using four-part paths:

In our environment, sales transactions reside natively in BigQuery:

We can now run a single SQL query joining our native sales transactions with customer records in Snowflake, product lines in Databricks, and store locations in AWS Glue:

BigQuery processes the joins in place. Notice that Snowflake identifiers appear in uppercase (

CORE.DIM_CUSTOMERS
), while Databricks and AWS Glue maintain lowercase table paths.

Figure 2 - Query results combining data across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue.

Explore cross-cloud data with natural language

Because federated Iceberg tables behave like native tables within BigQuery, downstream analytical features inherit access directly. You can point conversational analytics in BigQuery at these federated schemas to let team members explore cross-cloud data using natural language prompts.

To give conversational analytics full operational context, we save our federated join as a logical view:

Analyze sales performance in natural language

When you ask conversational analytics in BigQuery:

"Who are our top customers by total sales revenue, what products did they buy, and which stores did they shop at?"

Conversational analytics evaluates the schema across all three remote catalogs, generates the SQL statement, executes the query, and presents the response.

Figure 3: Conversational analytics in BigQuery translates plain-language prompts into federated queries across Snowflake, Databricks, and AWS Glue.

Plan for caching and data residency

Before deploying federated catalogs in production, consider these operational behaviors:

  • Background refresh timing: The 

    --refresh-interval
    flag controls metadata synchronization. The minimum interval is 300 seconds. For larger catalogs containing hundreds of tables, metadata retrieval can take longer. If a sync cycle overruns, BigQuery skips the next scheduled run to avoid task queuing.

  • Automatic query caching: BigQuery caches retrieved cross-cloud data blocks in the region where your federated catalog resides (e.g. 

    us-central1
    ). This helps reduce network transfer on repeated queries. Because cached blocks reside within Google Cloud storage in that region, confirm that this aligns with your organization's data residency policies.

  • Encryption controls: Cross-cloud cache blocks use Google-managed encryption keys. If your organization enforces the 

    constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices
    policy constraint, BigQuery bypasses the cache and reads directly from remote storage for every query.

  • Monitoring access metrics: You can evaluate cache utilization in your query execution plans. Check the 

    objectStorageStats
    section in BigQuery job statistics to compare 
    cacheBytesRead
    against 
    objectStorageBytesRead
    .

Next steps

In summary, Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse helps you activate your data regardless of where it lives without costly migrations or building additional data pipelines.   Get started today by reviewing the borderless Lakehouse architecture documentation to learn more about supported regions and credential configurations. You can work through the borderless Lakehouse codelab to practice federating external catalogs step-by-step. Finally, connect with your Google Cloud account team or customer engineer to evaluate borderless lakehouse patterns for your specific data platforms or industries.
